external_sources.title: Soil Basics — Illinois Extension
external_sources.content: A typical mineral soil is commonly described as approximately 45% mineral matter, 5% organic matter, 25% air and 25% water. The 5% organic-matter fraction should not be relabelled as all living organisms; this differs from the supplied school source, which labels its 5% fraction as soil living organisms. The discrepancy is retained for subject-lead review rather than silently changing the original source.

evidence.locator: Soil Basics, soil composition section
evidence.explanation: Supports the comparison of the common mineral-soil composition model with the 5% label in the supplied school source.

external_sources.rights: Factual summary paraphrased for educational context; no protected text or figures reproduced.
external_sources.attribution: University of Illinois Extension, Soil Basics.

external_sources.title: Physical Properties — FAO Soils Portal
external_sources.content: FAO describes soil texture as determined by the mineral components sand, silt and clay. Texture affects the retention of water and nutrients. Soil structure is formed when textural components aggregate into peds; structure affects aeration, water movement, heat transfer, root growth and resistance to erosion.

evidence.locator: Physical Properties, Soil Structure and Soil Texture sections
evidence.explanation: Supports the distinction between soil texture and structure and their effects on water, air, roots and erosion.

external_sources.rights: Factual summary paraphrased for educational context; no protected text or figures reproduced.
external_sources.attribution: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, FAO Soils Portal.

external_sources.title: National Agronomy Manual — Soil Texture
external_sources.content: The USDA National Agronomy Manual explains that soil texture is based on the relative percentages of sand, silt and clay. Particles larger than 2 mm are rock fragments, while the fine-earth fraction is smaller than 2 mm. Coarse-textured soils generally allow faster water percolation, while finer-textured soils retain more water; structure and compaction also affect movement of air and water.

evidence.locator: Part 508, Soil Texture and Soil Structure
evidence.explanation: Supports the comparison of particle-size conventions and the relationship between texture, water movement and compaction.

external_sources.rights: Factual summary paraphrased for educational context; no protected text or figures reproduced.
external_sources.attribution: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service, National Agronomy Manual, Part 508.

external_sources.title: Soil Acidity and Aglime — Penn State Extension
external_sources.content: Penn State Extension explains that agricultural liming materials neutralize soil acidity, commonly through carbonates, oxides or hydroxides. Calcium sulfate (gypsum) and magnesium sulfate are not liming materials because they do not neutralize soil acidity. Lime recommendations should be based on a soil test.

evidence.locator: Aglime Materials section
evidence.explanation: Supports the technical review of the school's listing of gypsum as a liming material.

external_sources.rights: Factual summary paraphrased for educational context; no protected text or figures reproduced.
external_sources.attribution: Penn State Extension, Soil Acidity and Aglime.

external_sources.title: Soil Texture Analysis — The Jar Test
external_sources.content: Clemson Extension's soil-texture jar test uses a clear straight-sided jar, sieved soil, water, shaking and timed settling. Sand settles first; after about two hours the silt layer is marked; after about 48 hours the clay layer is marked. The layer heights can be measured and used with a soil texture triangle to estimate the soil's textural class. The procedure is a classroom estimate, not a laboratory particle-size analysis.

evidence.locator: Soil Texture Analysis — The Jar Test, Procedure
evidence.explanation: Supports the detailed steps and timing in the authored sedimentation practical.

external_sources.rights: Factual summary paraphrased for educational context; no protected text or figures reproduced.
external_sources.attribution: Clemson Cooperative Extension, Home & Garden Information Center, Soil Texture Analysis — The Jar Test.

external_sources.title: Power Take-Off (PTO) Safety — Penn State Extension
external_sources.content: Penn State Extension explains that a tractor power take-off (PTO) shaft transfers mechanical power from the tractor to an implement. PTO entanglement is a serious hazard: keep all guards and shields in place, disengage the PTO and shut off the tractor before cleaning, adjusting or servicing machinery, never step over a rotating shaft, and wear close-fitting clothing.

evidence.locator: PTO Safety Practices
evidence.explanation: Supports the correction to the source's PTO function and the safety instructions for rotating driveline parts.

external_sources.rights: Factual summary paraphrased for educational context; no protected text or figures reproduced.
external_sources.attribution: Penn State Extension, Power Take-Off (PTO) Safety.

external_sources.title: Safe Tractor Operations: Tractor Operator Checklist — UF/IFAS Extension
external_sources.content: UF/IFAS Safe Tractor Operations emphasizes safe operators, safe tractors and safe working environments. Operators should use a seat belt when a rollover protective structure (ROPS) is fitted, keep extra riders off the tractor, reduce speed on slopes and rough surfaces, avoid ditches and holes, maintain visibility, check equipment and follow the operator's manual.

evidence.locator: Safe Tractor Operations, operator checklist
evidence.explanation: Supports safe tractor operation, inspection and rollover precautions.

external_sources.rights: Factual summary paraphrased for educational context; no protected text or figures reproduced.
external_sources.attribution: UF/IFAS Extension, Safe Tractor Operations: Tractor Operator Checklist.

external_sources.title: Frequently Asked Questions: Farm Machinery — Tamil Nadu Agricultural University
external_sources.content: Tamil Nadu Agricultural University guidance for farm machinery and sprayer use recommends protective clothing, gloves and masks; keeping people and animals out of the downwind spray path; never spraying against the wind; never clearing a blocked nozzle with the mouth; preventing spray drift into ponds, streams and wells; avoiding eating or smoking during spraying; and washing equipment and the operator after use.

evidence.locator: Farm Machinery FAQ, sprayer safety precautions
evidence.explanation: Supports the sprayer safety precautions and post-application cleaning guidance.

external_sources.rights: Factual summary paraphrased for educational context; no protected text or figures reproduced.

external_sources.title: Agriculture Paper 2, WASSCE (PC), 2018 — Examiner Report
external_sources.content: WAEC's 2018 Agricultural Science Paper 2 examiner report defines farm surveying as measuring and mapping a farm's position, height, size and boundaries. It gives the importance of determining farm area, preparing feasibility studies, identifying gradients and building locations, supporting farm planning and soil classification, and records uses for ranging poles, Gunter's chain, prismatic compass, measuring tape and theodolite.

evidence.locator: Question 1 and examiner observation/expected answers
evidence.explanation: Provides an official exam reference for farm surveying meaning, importance and common instrument uses.

external_sources.content: NIST Handbook 44 Appendix C states the exact area conversion: one hectare (ha) equals 10,000 square metres and 0.01 square kilometre.

evidence.locator: Appendix C, Units of Area, 1 hectare (ha)

external_sources.title: Selecting an Irrigation System — USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service
external_sources.content: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service distinguishes surface, sprinkler, drip or micro-irrigation, and subsurface systems. Surface irrigation moves water by gravity across the field; sprinkler systems distribute pressurised water through nozzles; drip/micro systems apply low-volume water near the crop through emitters. System choice depends on water quantity and quality, soil, slope, crop and field conditions.

evidence.locator: Four Classes of Irrigation Systems; Selecting an Irrigation System
evidence.explanation: Supports the technical distinction between sprinkler and drip/micro-irrigation and the factors used to select a system.

external_sources.rights: Factual summary paraphrased for educational context; no protected text or figures reproduced.
external_sources.attribution: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service, Small Scale Solutions for your Farm: Selecting an Irrigation System.

external_sources.title: Water Quality for Agriculture — Salinity Problems
external_sources.content: FAO explains that irrigation water contains dissolved salts and that root-zone salinity depends on irrigation-water quality, irrigation management and drainage adequacy. Leaching may be needed to move salts below the root zone, but it works only with adequate drainage; excess irrigation and poor drainage can raise the water table and worsen salinity or waterlogging.

evidence.locator: Chapter 2, Salinity Problems; drainage and leaching discussion
evidence.explanation: Supports the correction that irrigation does not automatically reduce salt and that leaching must be paired with adequate drainage.

external_sources.rights: Factual summary paraphrased for educational context; no protected text or figures reproduced.
external_sources.attribution: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, Water Quality for Agriculture.

external_sources.title: What's the Difference Between Climate and Weather? — NOAA
external_sources.content: NOAA explains climate as the average pattern of weather in a place over a long period, commonly 30 years or more. Climate descriptions use long-term observations such as temperature, precipitation, humidity, sunshine and wind. Drought is a recurring climate hazard and is distinct from the normal day-to-day weather.

evidence.locator: Climate definition and climate elements
evidence.explanation: Supports the distinction between long-term climate and short-term weather and the treatment of drought as a climate-related hazard.

external_sources.rights: Factual summary paraphrased for educational context; no protected text or figures reproduced.
external_sources.attribution: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, What's the Difference Between Climate and Weather?

external_sources.title: Soil Biology Primer — USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service
external_sources.content: USDA NRCS's Soil Biology Primer describes soil bacteria, fungi, protozoa, nematodes, arthropods and earthworms as living components of soil. Soil organisms contribute to decomposition and nutrient cycling, influence soil structure and water availability, and can affect crop pests, diseases and agricultural productivity. Not all soil organisms are harmful.

evidence.locator: Soil Biology Primer, soil organisms and agricultural productivity
evidence.explanation: Supports the distinction between beneficial soil organisms and harmful pests or pathogens.

external_sources.rights: Factual summary paraphrased for educational context; no protected text or figures reproduced.
external_sources.attribution: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service, Soil Biology Primer.

external_sources.title: Plant Nutrition for Food Security — FAO
external_sources.content: FAO's Plant Nutrition for Food Security identifies nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium and sulphur as macronutrients, and boron, iron, manganese, copper, molybdenum, chlorine and zinc as micronutrients. It explains that essential plant nutrients are required in sufficient amounts for healthy growth and yield, while carbon, hydrogen and oxygen are obtained from air and water rather than mineral soil sources.

evidence.locator: Essential plant nutrients and nutrient functions
evidence.explanation: Supports the distinction between macro- and micronutrients and the essential-element list.

external_sources.rights: Factual summary paraphrased for educational context; no protected table or text reproduced.
external_sources.attribution: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, Plant Nutrition for Food Security: A Guide for Integrated Nutrient Management.

external_sources.title: Nutrient Deficiencies — Royal Horticultural Society
external_sources.content: The Royal Horticultural Society explains that plants require macronutrients and micronutrients in different amounts and that deficiency symptoms can overlap with drought, waterlogging, light deprivation and other growing problems. Accurate diagnosis may require soil or plant-tissue analysis rather than relying on a single visible symptom.

evidence.locator: Nutrient deficiencies, symptoms and diagnostic caution
evidence.explanation: Supports the nutrient deficiency supplement and the warning not to diagnose from one symptom alone.

external_sources.rights: Factual summary paraphrased for educational context; no protected text or figures reproduced.

external_sources.title: Carbon Cycle — NOAA
external_sources.content: NOAA describes the carbon cycle as movement of carbon among the atmosphere, living organisms, soils, oceans and other reservoirs. Photosynthesis moves carbon dioxide into plant biomass; respiration, decomposition and combustion return carbon to the atmosphere or other pools.

evidence.locator: Carbon storage and exchange; photosynthesis, respiration and decomposition
evidence.explanation: Supports the carbon-cycle explanation and correction of oversimplified carbon-loss claims.

external_sources.rights: Factual summary paraphrased for educational context; no protected text or figures reproduced.
external_sources.attribution: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, Carbon Cycle.

external_sources.title: Water Cycle — U.S. Geological Survey
external_sources.content: USGS describes the water cycle through evaporation, evapotranspiration, condensation, precipitation, runoff, infiltration, groundwater recharge and groundwater flow. Solar energy drives evaporation and gravity moves water downhill and through soil.

evidence.locator: Water-cycle fluxes and movement between stores
evidence.explanation: Supports the corrected water-cycle processes and the distinction between transpiration and minor respiration contributions.

external_sources.rights: Factual summary paraphrased for educational context; no protected text or figures reproduced.

units.title: Soil: Meaning, Types, Composition and Properties
objectives: Define soil and explain its importance to plant growth.
Distinguish sandy, clayey and loamy soils by texture, drainage, water holding and aeration.
Explain the source's soil-composition figures and identify the unresolved 5% label discrepancy.
Recommend suitable practices for improving or protecting sandy and clayey soils.
units.body:
# Week 1 — Soil: meaning, types, composition and properties

## What soil is and why farmers study it
Soil is the loose, weathered material forming the upper layer of the land in which plants root and grow. It anchors plants and supplies water, air and mineral nutrients. Soil is not simply ground-up rock: it also contains organic matter, pore spaces, water, air and living organisms. Its properties influence which crops can grow well and how a farmer should manage the land.

## Three broad soil types in the school source
**Sandy soil** contains a high proportion of large sand particles. It feels gritty, has relatively large pore spaces, drains quickly and is usually well aerated. It holds less water and may lose soluble nutrients through leaching. The source notes cassava, cotton and groundnut as examples of crops grown on sandy soil. Because loose soil can be washed or blown away when bare, protect it with cover crops and mulch.

**Clayey soil** contains a high proportion of very fine particles. It feels smooth when dry and sticky when wet. Its small pore spaces allow it to hold much water, but drainage and air movement are slower. Wet clay can be moulded into a ribbon or cast; when it dries it may become hard. Add suitable organic matter to improve its structure. Apply lime only when a soil test or reliable assessment confirms that acidity needs correction.

**Loamy soil** is a workable mixture of sand, silt and clay with useful organic matter. It is generally crumbly, easier to cultivate than heavy clay, and can hold water while still allowing drainage and aeration. These balanced properties make loam suitable for many crops, although crop choice must still consider climate, nutrients, drainage and the crop's needs.

## Compare the soils
| Property | Sandy | Clayey | Loamy |
|---|---|---|---|
| Feel | Gritty | Smooth; sticky when wet | Crumbly and workable |
| Pore spaces | Generally larger | Generally smaller | A useful mixture |
| Drainage | Fast | Slow | Moderate when well structured |
| Water holding | Low | High | Moderate |
| Aeration | Usually good | Can be poor when wet/compacted | Usually favourable |
| Management priority | Add organic matter; keep soil covered | Improve structure and drainage | Maintain organic matter and avoid compaction |

## Managing sandy and clayey soils
For sandy soil, the school source recommends cover crops, compost or farmyard manure, mulching and avoiding bush burning. These practices add or protect organic matter and reduce the time bare soil is exposed. For clayey soil, organic manure can improve aggregation and workability. Do not apply lime automatically: it is a remedy for excessive acidity, not a universal soil conditioner.

## Soil composition — a source discrepancy to resolve
The supplied school note lists 45% mineral matter, 25% water, 25% air and 5% “soil living organisms”. A commonly used model for a typical mineral soil instead lists about 45% mineral matter, 5% organic matter, 25% water and 25% air. Organic matter and living organisms are related, but they are not interchangeable labels. This lesson preserves the school-source wording as evidence and flags the 5% label for subject-lead review; it must not be silently changed in the student release.

## Check your understanding
You should be able to define soil, compare sandy/clayey/loamy soil, explain why loam is often useful for crop production, and name practices that improve or protect sandy and clayey soils.

practice.question: Give five differences between sandy and clayey soil.
practice.answer: Sandy soil has larger, gritty particles; clayey soil has very fine particles. Sandy soil drains quickly; clayey soil drains slowly. units.subject: Agricultural Science
units.title: Soil Formation, Texture, Structure, pH and Profile
objectives: Name and explain the five major soil-forming factors.
Distinguish physical, chemical and biological weathering.
Differentiate soil texture from soil structure and explain their effects.
Interpret soil pH and describe the source's simplified A–D soil profile.
Describe a safe settling-jar demonstration and state its limitations.
units.body:
# Week 2 — Soil formation and soil properties

## Factors that form soil
The school source identifies five major soil-forming factors: **climate, parent material, topography (relief), biotic factors (organisms) and time**. Climate acts through temperature, rainfall and wind. Heating and cooling can make rock expand and contract; rain and moving water weather and transport material. Parent material is the rock or material from which soil develops and influences its mineral character. Topography affects runoff, erosion, drainage and the depth of soil that accumulates. Roots, earthworms, termites and microorganisms help break material, mix soil and decompose organic residues. Soil formation takes time; a young soil and a mature soil may have different profiles and properties.

## Weathering: breaking rock into smaller material
Weathering is the breakdown or alteration of rock at or near the Earth's surface. **Physical weathering** breaks rock into smaller pieces without changing its basic mineral composition; examples include repeated heating and cooling, ice expanding in cracks, and abrasion by moving water or wind-blown particles. **Chemical weathering** changes minerals through reactions such as solution, carbonation, hydration, hydrolysis and oxidation. **Biological weathering** results from living things: roots widen cracks, burrowing animals disturb material, and microorganisms decompose organic matter. These processes work together; they are not separate stages that always occur in a fixed order.

## Texture and structure are different
**Soil texture** describes the relative amounts and sizes of mineral particles, especially sand, silt and clay. The school note gives this particle-size table: clay below 0.002 mm; silt 0.002–0.02 mm; fine sand 0.02–0.2 mm; coarse sand 0.2–2.0 mm; gravel above 2 mm. Other established classification systems use different boundaries—for example, the USDA system places silt between 0.002 and 0.05 mm and treats particles above 2 mm as rock fragments. Keep the school's table identified as its source convention until the subject lead approves which classification the class should use.

**Soil structure** describes how particles are arranged into aggregates. Structure affects air spaces, water movement, root growth and erosion. The source lists single-grained, crumb, plate-like, spheroidal, prismatic and block-like structures. Cover crops, organic manure, mulching and avoiding overgrazing help protect soil structure; working wet soil or compacting it can damage aggregates.

## Soil pH and the soil profile
Soil pH indicates acidity or alkalinity. A pH below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral and above 7 is alkaline. Strong acidity can restrict nutrient availability and crop growth. The source lists leaching, acid-forming fertilizers, parent material and plant nutrient uptake among possible causes. Liming materials may be used to correct acidity, but the material and rate should be selected from a soil test. The source's list includes gypsum among liming materials; this needs technical review because gypsum is not a general substitute for agricultural lime when correcting soil acidity.

A **soil profile** is a vertical section showing layers called horizons. The supplied school note uses a simplified A–D description: A is topsoil, B is subsoil where some materials accumulate, C is partly weathered parent material, and D is bedrock. Soil-survey systems may use additional horizon labels, so use the class source's A–D model for this exercise and ask the teacher before comparing systems.

**Figure/source alignment check:** The embedded profile figures do not all use the written A–D labels. One diagram labels humus, topsoil, subsoil, weathered rock fragments and bedrock; another uses O, A, B, C and R horizons. The soil-structure figures also use labels such as granular, massive and columnar, while the text uses crumb and spheroidal. The figures have been located, but the subject lead must approve the vocabulary and reconcile each diagram with the written lesson before release.

## Safe practical investigation: a settling jar
**Materials:** a clear straight-sided jar with a tight lid, a small soil sample, a sieve or mesh strainer, clean water, a ruler and a marker.

1. Under the teacher's direction, remove stones, roots and large debris by passing the soil through a coarse sieve. Break up large clods.
2. Fill about one-third of the jar with the prepared soil. Add clean water, leaving space at the top.
3. Close the lid firmly and shake until the soil and water form a well-mixed suspension. Place the jar on a level surface where it will not be disturbed.
4. Mark the top of the settled sand after about 1 minute. Mark the top of the silt layer after about 2 hours. Leave the jar for about 48 hours, then mark the top of the clay layer. Some organic fragments may float.
5. Measure the thickness of each layer and the total settled soil. Estimate each percentage using: layer thickness ÷ total soil-layer thickness × 100. If the class has studied the soil-texture triangle, use the three percentages to estimate the textural class.
6. Draw and label the layers. In the authored diagram, sand is at the bottom, then silt, then clay; water is above the settled soil and some organic material may float.

**Safety and limitations:** Work under teacher supervision, keep the lid tight while shaking, do not taste soil or bring it near the eyes, and wash hands after handling samples. This is a classroom estimate, not a laboratory particle-size analysis. Aggregates, organic matter and incomplete dispersion can affect the layers and the estimated percentages.

Other experiments named in the school source include tests for moisture content, porosity or water-holding capacity, capillarity, soil organisms and organic matter. The source lists these activities but does not provide full procedures; each needs a teacher-approved method, apparatus list and safety check before practical delivery.

## Check your understanding
You should be able to name and explain the five soil-forming factors, distinguish physical/chemical/biological weathering, tell texture from structure, interpret pH, describe the simplified soil profile, and explain what a settling-jar demonstration can and cannot show.

practice.question: Describe the sedimentation experiment with the aid of a diagram.
practice.answer_locator: Authored model answer, explanation and marking guide; subject review pending.
practice.answer: Sieve the soil to remove stones and roots. Put soil into a clear jar until it is about one-third full, add water leaving headspace, close and shake thoroughly. Leave the jar level and undisturbed. Mark the sand layer after about 1 minute, the silt layer after about 2 hours and the clay layer after about 48 hours. Measure the layer thicknesses, calculate each percentage as layer thickness divided by total soil-layer thickness multiplied by 100, and use a soil-texture triangle if taught. Refer to the labelled sedimentation-jar diagram in this package.
practice.explanation: The procedure is based on the cited Clemson Extension jar test and is a classroom estimate, not a laboratory analysis. The diagram shows the general order of settled layers; actual thicknesses vary by sample and preparation.

Adds soil and water with space at the top.
Closes and shakes the jar, then leaves it undisturbed.

units.body:
# Week 3 — Farm machinery and implements

## What farm machinery means

Farm machinery includes the machines and implements used to prepare land, plant crops, care for crops, harvest produce and handle farm products. Some machines supply power; others are attached to a tractor or operated by hand. Examples in the school source include tractors, ploughs, harrows, cultivators, ridgers, planters, harvesters, shellers, dryers, sprayers, incubators and milking machines.

## The tractor

A tractor is a powerful, multipurpose farm vehicle used to move loads and to supply power for suitable implements. A tractor may pull a trailer, operate a pump, carry or lift a mounted implement, or drive a machine through its power take-off (PTO).

### Main parts and what they do

- **Engine:** supplies the power. A diesel engine normally uses compression ignition and does not use spark plugs; a petrol engine uses spark plugs. The school source's statement that both fuel types operate without spark plugs needs correction.
- **Power take-off (PTO) shaft:** transfers rotary mechanical power from the tractor to a compatible implement, such as a mower or baler. It is not the part used to pull an implement.
- **Drawbar or approved hitch:** provides the correct coupling point for pulling a trailer or trailed implement. Never attach a heavy load above the approved drawbar point.
- **Hydraulic control system:** raises, lowers or controls suitable mounted implements.
- **Wheels and tyres:** support the tractor, provide traction and allow movement. Tyre pressure and condition affect safe operation.

**Important correction to the source:** The PTO transfers power; the drawbar or hitch pulls a trailed implement. Keep these functions distinct.

### Functions of a tractor

A tractor can:
1. pull a trailer for transporting farm inputs and produce;
2. pull suitable tillage implements;
3. power water pumps and other equipment;
4. operate a planter, sprayer, mower or harvester when correctly coupled;
5. provide power for other approved farm operations.

The tractor performs only the task for which the implement and coupling are designed. Operators must follow the tractor and implement manuals.

### Daily maintenance

Before or after the day's work, as directed by the operator's manual:
- remove mud, crop trash and debris;
- check engine oil, coolant and other fluid levels;
- inspect tyres and check pressure;
- check the battery and electrical connections;
- look for fuel, oil or hydraulic leaks;
- check lights, brakes, steering and safety guards;
- report faults and do not operate unsafe equipment.

### Periodic maintenance

At the manufacturer's service intervals:
- change engine oil and filters as specified;
- service or replace air and fuel filters;
- inspect and replace worn tyres and damaged parts;
- tighten loose nuts, bolts and shields;
- inspect belts, hoses, brakes, steering and hydraulic lines;
- lubricate specified moving parts;
- keep a service record and follow the operator's manual.

Never service, clean, unblock or adjust a PTO-driven machine while the engine is running or the PTO is engaged.

## Bulldozers and tree pullers

A bulldozer is a powerful tracked machine with a broad blade at the front. It can push soil, clear vegetation, remove stumps and level ground. It can also be expensive, compact soil, damage soil structure, remove fertile topsoil, increase erosion risk and disturb the land.

A tree puller is designed to uproot or remove trees and stumps. Compared with indiscriminate bulldozing, a suitable tree-pulling method can disturb less soil, retain more topsoil and organic matter, reduce compaction and lower the risk of erosion. The method and machine must still be selected for the site and used safely.

## Other farm machines

- **Sheller:** separates grain or seeds from a cob, pod, husk or other covering. Use the correct machine setting for the crop.
- **Dryer:** reduces moisture in harvested crops or animal products to help safe storage and handling.
- **Incubator:** provides controlled conditions for hatching fertilised eggs artificially.
- **Milking machine:** extracts milk mechanically from the udder of a dairy animal. Equipment must be cleaned and sanitised as directed.
- **Planter:** places seed at a planned rate, spacing and depth. Types listed in the source include broadcast, row-crop, precision and grain-drill planters.
- **Harvester:** cuts or gathers mature crops. Examples include mower-type, forage and combine harvesters.
- **Sprayer:** applies a measured liquid, such as an approved crop-protection product or foliar feed. Types named in the source include knapsack, tractor-mounted and aircraft-mounted sprayers.

## Tractor-coupled implements

A tractor-coupled implement is attached to a tractor so that the tractor can pull it, lift it or supply power to it.

### Ploughs — primary tillage

A plough is used for primary tillage: the first major loosening and turning of soil during land preparation. The source names:
- **Disc plough:** uses rotating concave discs to cut and turn soil.
- **Mouldboard plough:** uses a share to cut the furrow slice and a mouldboard to lift and turn it.

The main parts and their functions should be learned from a teacher-approved labelled diagram and the implement manual. Do not guess an unlabeled part from a photograph.

### Harrows and cultivators — secondary tillage

A harrow is used after ploughing to break clods, level the surface and prepare a finer seedbed. A spring-tine cultivator is a secondary-tillage implement. It can loosen the surface, break clods, uproot small weeds and bring stones or roots to the surface without turning the soil completely over.

### Ridgers

A ridger forms ridges or raised rows for crops that are planted or grown on ridges. The source identifies disc and mouldboard ridgers. It is generally used after the soil has been ploughed and harrowed, according to the crop and field plan.

### Planters, harvesters and sprayers

Planters place seeds; harvesters collect mature crops; sprayers apply liquid materials. Their settings, guards and attachments differ. Always identify the machine, read its instructions and use the correct implement for the task.

## Safe operation of tractors, PTOs and sprayers

- Only a trained, authorised person should operate a tractor or powered implement.
- Read the operator's manual and check the machine before starting.
- Keep guards and shields in place. Keep people, especially children, away from moving machinery.
- Use the seat belt when the tractor has a rollover protective structure (ROPS); do not carry extra riders.
- Reduce speed on slopes, rough or slippery ground and when turning. Keep away from ditches and unstable edges.
- Disengage the PTO, stop the engine and wait for all moving parts to stop before connecting, cleaning, unclogging or servicing an implement.
- Never step over a rotating PTO shaft. Keep loose clothing, hair and hands away from rotating parts.
- When spraying, wear the protective clothing and equipment specified on the product label. Do not spray against the wind; keep people and animals out of the downwind area.
- Never clear a blocked nozzle with the mouth. Do not eat, drink or smoke while mixing or spraying.
- Prevent spray from entering wells, ponds, streams or drains. Clean equipment and wash after use according to the label and teacher's instructions.

## Practical activities

1. With a teacher-approved diagram or safe display model, identify the main parts of a tractor and explain the function of the engine, PTO, drawbar/hitch and hydraulic system.
2. Compare a disc plough and a mouldboard plough. Draw and label their main parts only after checking the labels with a teacher or reliable implement manual.
3. Draw a knapsack sprayer and label its tank, pump/lever, hose, lance, trigger valve and nozzle.
4. For each machine studied, state its use, one maintenance requirement and one safety precaution.

## Check your understanding

You should be able to define farm machinery, explain tractor functions and maintenance, distinguish PTO power transmission from drawbar pulling, compare bulldozers and tree pullers, identify common farm machines and tractor-coupled implements, and state safe operating precautions.

units.title: Farm Surveying and Planning of Farmstead
objectives: Define farm surveying and explain its importance to farm management.
Identify common surveying instruments and state their uses.
Describe precautions during chaining and maintenance of surveying equipment.
Define farm planning and farmstead and explain why planning matters.
Explain factors that influence farmstead siting and safe layout.
Calculate areas of rectangles, triangles and trapeziums using consistent units.
Calculate planting stands and plant population from area and spacing.
units.body:
# Weeks 4–5 — Farm surveying and planning of the farmstead

## Meaning of farm surveying

Farm surveying is the systematic measurement and mapping of a farm's position, boundaries, area, distances, levels, angles and physical features. The measurements are used to prepare a plan or map that helps the farmer understand the land and make decisions about its use.

## Importance of farm surveying

Farm surveying:
1. establishes and records the farm's boundaries and area;
2. supports feasibility studies and farm investment decisions;
3. helps the farmer use land appropriately;
4. assists with the location of farm buildings, roads, drains and fields;
5. provides information for farm maps and soil maps;
6. supports soil classification and land evaluation;
7. helps estimate gradients and plan drainage or irrigation;
8. provides records for land registration, ownership or loan applications where accepted;
9. supports planning and future production estimates.

A survey plan records measured information. It does not by itself guarantee land ownership, a loan or a certificate of occupancy; those depend on the relevant legal and administrative requirements.

## Common farm-surveying equipment and uses

### Ranging pole
A ranging pole is a straight pole, usually made of wood, metal or another durable material. It may be about 1.8 m, 2.4 m or 3 m long and is painted in contrasting colours so that it can be seen from a distance. Its pointed end can be placed at a survey station. It is used to mark stations and to help the survey team establish a straight line between points.

### Gunter's chain
A Gunter's chain is a metal survey chain made of linked sections. The traditional chain is 66 feet long, approximately 20.12 m (often rounded to 20.13 m), and has 100 links. It is used to measure distances along a survey line. Keep it straight and properly aligned; a sagging, kinked or incorrectly counted chain produces inaccurate measurements.

### Measuring tape
A measuring tape may be made of steel, fibreglass or another suitable material. It is wound in a case and marked in metric units, and some tapes also show imperial units. It is used for measuring lengths, widths, heights and short offsets. Read the correct scale and keep the tape properly aligned and tensioned.

### Prismatic compass
A prismatic compass contains a magnetic compass card and a sighting arrangement. It is used to determine the bearing or direction of a survey line. Keep it away from magnetic objects and follow the instrument's instructions when taking a reading.

### Theodolite
A theodolite is a precision surveying instrument mounted on a tripod. It is used to measure horizontal and vertical angles. It must be levelled and handled carefully; a damaged or poorly adjusted instrument can give inaccurate readings.

### Arrows or pins
Survey arrows are thin pointed metal pins, often with a ring at one end and a visible marker. They are used during chaining to mark the end of each chain length and to identify measured points.

### Offset staff
An offset staff is a graduated rod used to measure short offsets from a survey line to a boundary, feature or object. Some designs have a hook to help retrieve a chain through a hedge or obstruction.

### Beacon or pillar
A beacon is a durable marker, often a concrete block or pillar, placed at a surveyed point. Its identifying mark is kept visible above ground. It helps preserve and identify a measured boundary or reference point.

## Precautions when chaining a farm

- Check the chain or tape for damage before starting.
- Keep the chain or tape straight, taut and properly aligned with the survey line.
- Avoid kinks, twists and unnecessary sag.
- Make sure the correct end and link count are used.
- Mark each chain length with an arrow or pin and record it immediately in the field book.
- Read the scale at eye level to reduce parallax error.
- Repeat doubtful measurements and check the arithmetic before preparing the plan.

## General maintenance of surveying instruments

After use, remove soil and moisture, dry the equipment and store it in a clean, cool and dry place. Keep metal parts lightly protected against rust where the manufacturer permits. Protect compass cards, theodolite lenses and other precision parts from scratches, knocks, rain and excessive heat. Store chains and tapes without kinks, replace worn or damaged parts, and use each instrument only for its intended purpose. Only trained users should adjust precision instruments.

## Meaning of farm planning and farmstead

Farm planning is the process of deciding how the available farm land, buildings, water, labour, roads and other resources will be arranged and used. A farmstead is the farm house together with the buildings and structures used for farm production, storage and processing. It may include a dwelling, stores, livestock houses, machinery sheds, workshops and processing areas.

## Importance of farm planning

Good farm planning helps the farmer:
- use land, labour, buildings and other resources efficiently;
- place buildings and structures where they can be reached and serviced;
- coordinate crop, livestock, storage and processing operations;
- reduce unnecessary movement, waste, pollution and conflict between activities;
- organise the farm to meet production and market needs.

## Factors to consider when siting a farmstead

Important factors include:
1. **Topography:** choose land that is suitable for building and allows safe access and drainage.
2. **Soil type and stability:** consider bearing capacity, erosion risk and suitability for the intended buildings or crops.
3. **Accessibility:** provide reliable access for workers, vehicles, inputs and produce.
4. **Water supply:** ensure a dependable and safe water source.
5. **Health and hygiene:** separate residential areas from sources of odour, waste, flies and disease.
6. **Market access:** consider distance and transport to buyers and suppliers.
7. **Drainage:** avoid flood-prone sites and provide safe drainage.
8. **Prevailing wind and biosecurity:** consider how wind may carry dust, odours or pathogens between buildings, and plan separation accordingly.

The source gives a simplified rule that livestock buildings should be placed on the poorest soil. Do not treat that as an absolute rule. Building sites must be safe, stable, well drained, accessible and suitable for the building; crop fields should be allocated according to soil capability and the farm plan.

## Measuring farm area and calculating plant population

### Area formulas

- Rectangle: area = length × breadth.
- Triangle: area = ½ × base × perpendicular height.
- Trapezium: area = ½ × (sum of the parallel sides) × perpendicular height.

Use the correct units throughout. Convert centimetres to metres before calculating an area in square metres.

**Important correction to the source:** one hectare is exactly 10,000 m², not 100,000 m².

### Plant spacing and population

Plant spacing is the distance between plants within a row and the distance between rows. If spacing is 30 cm × 30 cm, convert each distance to metres: 0.3 m × 0.3 m. The ground area allocated to one planting stand is therefore 0.09 m².

A basic estimate is:

**Number of planting stands = farm area ÷ area occupied by one stand**

**Total plant population = number of stands × number of plants per stand**

This estimate assumes the whole measured area is planted at the stated spacing. Headlands, paths, drains, buildings, irregular boundaries and unplanted areas reduce the actual number.

### Worked example from the source

A rectangular field is 60 m long and 30 m wide. Tomato spacing is 30 cm × 30 cm, with two plants per stand.

1. Field area = 60 m × 30 m = 1,800 m².
2. Convert spacing: 30 cm = 0.3 m.
3. Area per stand = 0.3 m × 0.3 m = 0.09 m².
4. Number of stands = 1,800 ÷ 0.09 = 20,000 stands.
5. Total plants = 20,000 × 2 = 40,000 tomato plants.

The result is a theoretical estimate. Adjust it if the field has paths, borders, drains, buildings or other unused space.

## Practical activities

1. In a safe school plot, identify a baseline and use ranging poles, a tape or chain and arrows to measure a simple rectangular area under teacher supervision.
2. Record the measurements in a field book, calculate the area and draw a simple plan with a scale, north arrow and labelled features.
3. Identify the eight surveying instruments described in this lesson and state one use and one care precaution for each.
4. Calculate the area of a rectangular, triangular or trapezoidal plot.
5. Calculate plant stands and total plant population from a stated field area, spacing and number of plants per stand.

practice.question: Describe surface and subsurface irrigation.
practice.answer_locator: Authored model answer, explanation and marking guide; subject review pending.
practice.answer: Surface irrigation moves water over the soil surface by gravity through furrows, basins, borders or channels. Subsurface irrigation supplies water below the soil surface through buried pipes or controlled water-table systems so that it reaches the crop root zone.
practice.explanation: Surface irrigation applies water on the land surface; subsurface irrigation delivers water below it. Do not confuse either with drainage, which removes excess water.

practice.question_locator: Authored practice: irrigation, leaching and drainage
practice.question: Explain why irrigation, leaching and drainage must be planned together when irrigation water contains dissolved salts.
practice.answer_locator: Authored model answer, explanation and marking guide; subject review pending.
practice.answer: Irrigation water adds salts to the soil. Leaching moves accumulated salts below the crop root zone, but the water carrying those salts must then be removed through adequate drainage. Without drainage, the water table may rise and salts can return to the root zone, causing waterlogging and reduced crop growth.
practice.explanation: The answer explains the sequence and the risk of poor drainage. Leaching is not effective as a salinity-control measure unless drainage can remove the water and salts.

marking.criterion: Identifies that irrigation water contains salts.
Explains leaching moves salts below the root zone.
Explains drainage removes the leaching water and salts.
Explains the risk of waterlogging or salt return if drainage is inadequate.

units.body:
# Weeks 8–9 — Plant nutrients, nutrient cycles and water in crop production

## Meaning and classification of plant nutrients

Plant nutrients are essential chemical elements that plants need to complete their life cycles and produce healthy growth. They are classified by the relative quantities required:

- **Macronutrients** are required in comparatively large amounts. The mineral macronutrients are nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), potassium (K), calcium (Ca), magnesium (Mg) and sulphur (S). Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium are often called primary macronutrients; calcium, magnesium and sulphur are secondary macronutrients.
- **Micronutrients** or trace elements are required in small amounts. They include iron (Fe), manganese (Mn), zinc (Zn), copper (Cu), boron (B), molybdenum (Mo), chlorine (Cl) and nickel (Ni).

Carbon (C), hydrogen (H) and oxygen (O) are also essential to plants, but plants obtain them mainly from carbon dioxide and water; they are not normally classified as mineral soil nutrients. A nutrient is not unimportant because a plant needs only a small amount of it. A shortage of any essential nutrient can limit growth and yield.

## Functions and deficiency symptoms of plant nutrients

The following table summarises common functions and symptoms. Symptoms can differ between crops and may resemble disease, drought, waterlogging, root damage or pH problems. Confirm suspected deficiencies with soil or plant-tissue testing and suitable technical advice before applying fertiliser.

| Nutrient | Main functions | Common deficiency symptoms |
|---|---|---|
| **Nitrogen (N)** | Needed for amino acids, proteins, nucleic acids and chlorophyll; supports leaf and stem growth. | Older leaves often become pale or yellow; plants are stunted and have reduced vegetative growth. |
| **Phosphorus (P)** | Part of ATP and nucleic acids; supports energy transfer, root development, flowering, seed formation and early growth. | Slow or stunted growth, poor roots, delayed maturity and sometimes dark-green or purplish older leaves. |
| **Potassium (K)** | Activates enzymes; regulates stomata and water balance; supports carbohydrate movement, stem strength and stress tolerance. | Yellowing or scorching at leaf margins, weak stems, poor growth and reduced stress tolerance. |
| **Calcium (Ca)** | Builds cell walls and membranes; supports cell division and growing points, especially in roots and young tissues. | Death or distortion of growing points, poor root tips, distorted young leaves and disorders such as blossom-end rot in susceptible fruit. |
| **Magnesium (Mg)** | Central component of chlorophyll; activates enzymes and supports phosphate and carbohydrate metabolism. | Interveinal chlorosis, often first on older leaves, followed by premature leaf fall in severe cases. |
| **Sulphur (S)** | Part of sulphur-containing amino acids and proteins; supports enzyme and vitamin functions. | Yellowing of younger leaves, stunted growth and delayed maturity; symptoms can resemble nitrogen deficiency. |
| **Iron (Fe)** | Required for electron-transfer enzymes and chlorophyll formation; it is not itself the central atom of chlorophyll. | Interveinal chlorosis, especially on young leaves; severe deficiency can make leaves very pale. |
| **Manganese (Mn)** | Activates enzymes and supports photosynthesis, including water-splitting in photosystem II. | Interveinal chlorosis and small brown or grey necrotic specks, often on younger leaves. |
| **Copper (Cu)** | Supports redox enzymes, photosynthesis, lignin formation and reproductive growth. | Shoot dieback, distorted or pale young leaves, poor flowering or grain formation and weak stems. |
| **Zinc (Zn)** | Activates enzymes and supports auxin formation, internode growth and protein metabolism. | Short internodes, small leaves, rosetting and interveinal chlorosis. |
| **Boron (B)** | Supports cell-wall formation, sugar transport, growing points, pollen-tube growth and fruit or seed development. | Death of growing points, brittle or distorted young tissues, poor flower/fruit set and hollow or cracked stems in some crops. |
| **Molybdenum (Mo)** | Part of nitrate-reductase and nitrogen-fixation enzymes; supports nitrogen metabolism. | Poor nitrogen use, yellowing and characteristic symptoms such as whiptail in cauliflower. |
| **Chlorine (Cl)** | Helps maintain osmotic balance and supports stomatal function and photosynthesis. | Deficiency is uncommon; may cause wilting, chlorosis or reduced root growth in susceptible crops. |
| **Nickel (Ni)** | Required for urease activity and normal nitrogen metabolism. | Deficiency is rare; may cause leaf-tip necrosis and poor seed or plant development. |

Nutrient deficiency symptoms are not a substitute for diagnosis. Soil pH, root health, moisture, temperature and interactions between nutrients can affect availability and uptake.

## Nitrogen cycle

The nitrogen cycle is the movement and transformation of nitrogen among the atmosphere, soil, plants, animals and microorganisms. Plants mainly absorb nitrogen as nitrate (NO₃⁻) or ammonium (NH₄⁺). Most atmospheric nitrogen gas (N₂) cannot be used directly by plants.

### Ways nitrogen enters or becomes available in soil

1. **Symbiotic nitrogen fixation:** nitrogen-fixing bacteria, such as suitable rhizobia in legume root nodules, convert atmospheric nitrogen into compounds that can enter the soil-plant system.
2. **Non-symbiotic fixation:** free-living or associative microorganisms fix some atmospheric nitrogen without forming the same root-nodule partnership.
3. **Atmospheric fixation:** lightning can form nitrogen oxides that return to land in rain; this is a natural but comparatively small input.
4. **Organic inputs:** manure, compost, dead roots, crop residues and other organic matter add nitrogen to soil.
5. **Fertiliser application and deposition:** nitrogen fertilisers and atmospheric deposition add nitrogen to the soil.

Ammonification and nitrification are transformations of nitrogen already present in organic matter or ammonium; they do not create new nitrogen in the soil.

### Main transformations in the nitrogen cycle

- **Decomposition and ammonification (mineralisation):** microorganisms break down organic nitrogen in residues, manure and dead organisms and release ammonium (NH₄⁺).
- **Nitrification:** under suitable, oxygenated conditions, microorganisms oxidise ammonium to nitrite (NO₂⁻), then other microorganisms oxidise nitrite to nitrate (NO₃⁻).
- **Assimilation:** plant roots take up nitrate or ammonium and use the nitrogen to make amino acids, proteins and other compounds. Animals obtain nitrogen by feeding on plants or other animals.
- **Denitrification:** under oxygen-poor conditions, microorganisms reduce nitrate and related compounds to gaseous nitrogen forms, including nitrogen gas (N₂) and nitrous oxide (N₂O), which can leave the soil.

### Nitrification in more detail

Nitrification is the biological oxidation of ammonium into nitrate in two main stages:

1. Ammonium (NH₄⁺) is oxidised to nitrite (NO₂⁻) by ammonia-oxidising microorganisms.
2. Nitrite (NO₂⁻) is oxidised to nitrate (NO₃⁻) by nitrite-oxidising microorganisms.

Nitrification generally requires oxygen and is affected by soil moisture, temperature and pH. It is different from ammonification, which releases ammonium from organic nitrogen.

### Ways nitrogen is lost from soil

Nitrogen can be lost through:
- **Denitrification:** nitrate is converted to gaseous nitrogen forms and released to the atmosphere.
- **Leaching:** soluble nitrate moves below the crop root zone with draining water.
- **Volatilisation:** nitrogen is lost as ammonia gas, especially when some fertilisers or manures are left on the soil surface under conditions that favour ammonia release.
- **Erosion and runoff:** nitrogen attached to soil particles or dissolved in runoff is carried away.
- **Crop and animal removal:** nitrogen leaves the field when harvested produce, fodder or animals are removed.
- **Burning:** fire can release nitrogen from vegetation and surface organic matter.

Soil pH, oxidation and reduction conditions influence nitrogen transformations and availability; they are not, by themselves, separate nitrogen-loss pathways.

## Carbon cycle

The carbon cycle is the movement of carbon among the atmosphere, plants, animals, soil, oceans and rocks.

1. Green plants and algae take in carbon dioxide (CO₂) during photosynthesis and use the carbon to build sugars and other organic compounds.
2. Animals obtain carbon by feeding on plants or other animals.
3. Plants, animals and microorganisms release carbon dioxide through respiration.
4. Decomposers break down dead organisms and wastes, returning carbon to the soil and atmosphere; some carbon becomes stored in soil organic matter.
5. Burning wood, crop residues and fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide and other gases.
6. Oceans exchange carbon dioxide with the atmosphere and store large amounts of carbon.

Carbon can also be stored for long periods in soil organic matter, sediments, carbonate minerals and fossil fuels. Leaching and drainage can move dissolved carbon compounds, but they are not the only or general explanation for carbon leaving agricultural soil.

## Water cycle

The water cycle is the continuous movement of water among the atmosphere, land, living organisms, rivers, lakes, oceans and underground stores. Solar energy drives evaporation; gravity helps move water downhill and through soil.

Main processes include:
1. **Evaporation:** liquid water changes to water vapour from oceans, lakes, rivers and soil.
2. **Transpiration:** plants release water vapour through their leaves.
3. **Condensation:** water vapour cools and forms tiny droplets or ice crystals in clouds.
4. **Precipitation:** water falls to the earth as rain, snow or other forms.
5. **Runoff:** water flows over the land into streams, rivers, lakes and oceans.
6. **Infiltration:** water enters the soil surface.
7. **Percolation:** water moves downward through soil and rock.
8. **Groundwater flow and storage:** water moves through and is stored in aquifers before returning to springs, rivers or the ocean.

Evapotranspiration combines evaporation from land and transpiration from plants. Plant and animal respiration also releases water vapour, but transpiration and evaporation are the major land-to-atmosphere pathways.

## Forms of water in the soil

- **Hygroscopic water:** a very thin film held tightly around soil particles. It is generally unavailable to plant roots.
- **Capillary water:** water held in small soil pores by capillary forces. It is usually the main form available to plants.
- **Gravitational water:** water that moves down through larger pores under gravity after the soil becomes saturated. It is generally temporary and may drain below the root zone.

The amount of each form depends on soil texture, structure, organic matter, rainfall, irrigation and drainage.

## Ways of conserving soil water

Farmers can conserve water by:
- reducing runoff through contour ridging, strip cropping, terracing or suitable field layout;
- adding organic matter to improve aggregation and water storage;
- applying mulch to reduce direct evaporation and protect the soil surface;
- using cover crops to protect soil and improve infiltration;
- controlling weeds so they do not compete with crops for water;
- using appropriate tillage and avoiding unnecessary soil disturbance;
- maintaining soil structure and preventing compaction;
- harvesting and storing rainwater where safe and practical.

The method should suit the crop, soil, slope and rainfall conditions. Water conservation does not mean keeping soil waterlogged.

## Importance of water to crops

Water:
1. dissolves mineral nutrients and provides the medium for their absorption by roots;
2. transports nutrients and other substances through plant tissues;
3. is a raw material for photosynthesis;
4. supports enzyme activity and metabolic reactions;
5. forms a major part of cell contents and protoplasm;
6. cools plants through transpiration;
7. maintains cell turgor, which supports leaves and stems;
8. is needed for seed imbibition and germination;
9. supports growth, transport and survival throughout the plant's life.

## Importance of organic matter in agriculture

Organic matter:
- supplies and slowly releases nutrients as it decomposes;
- improves soil aggregation and structure;
- increases water-holding capacity in many soils;
- supports soil organisms and nutrient cycling;
- helps protect the soil surface and reduce erosion;
- can improve nutrient retention and buffer some changes in soil conditions.

## Factors influencing nutrient availability in soil

Nutrient availability depends on more than the total nutrient content. Important factors include soil pH; soil moisture and aeration; temperature; soil texture and structure; organic matter and microbial activity; nutrient interactions; leaching or erosion; and healthy roots. Soil testing and crop-specific advice should guide nutrient management.

## Practical activities

1. Sort listed plant nutrients into macronutrients and micronutrients and identify the non-mineral essential elements carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
2. Use a nutrient-deficiency chart to match symptoms with possible nutrients, then explain why soil or tissue testing is needed before treatment.
3. Draw and explain the nitrogen cycle, labelling fixation, ammonification, nitrification, assimilation and denitrification.
4. Draw the carbon cycle and identify photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition and combustion.
5. Draw the water cycle and label evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, runoff, infiltration and percolation.
6. Compare hygroscopic, capillary and gravitational water and explain which form is generally available to roots.
7. Demonstrate or describe two soil-water conservation practices suitable for a school plot.

## Check your understanding

You should be able to classify plant nutrients; explain the functions and deficiency symptoms of major and trace nutrients; describe nitrogen transformations and losses; explain carbon and water cycles; identify forms of soil water; describe water conservation; and explain the importance of water and organic matter to crop production.

practice.question: Differentiate between nitrification and denitrification.
practice.answer_locator: Authored model answer, explanation and marking guide; subject review pending.

practice.explanation: The two processes have opposite directions in the nitrogen cycle and different oxygen requirements.

marking.criterion: Gives the ammonium → nitrite → nitrate sequence.
Identifies gaseous nitrogen products and oxygen-poor conditions.

practice.question: Why should a farmer not diagnose a nutrient deficiency from one visible leaf symptom alone?
practice.answer_locator: Authored model answer, explanation and marking guide; subject review pending.
practice.answer: Different nutrient deficiencies can produce similar symptoms, and drought, waterlogging, pests, disease, root damage or unsuitable pH can cause similar changes. Soil or plant-tissue testing and a field assessment help confirm the cause before fertiliser is applied.
practice.explanation: A symptom is evidence, not proof. Incorrect diagnosis can waste money and may worsen nutrient imbalance or environmental loss.

marking.criterion: Explains that deficiency symptoms can overlap.
Names another stress such as drought, disease or pH.
Explains why confirmation matters before fertiliser application.

open_items.required_action: Verify the figure labels against the written source, approve the vocabulary/profile model, confirm reuse rights, and replace the source-extract locators with stored asset files whose bytes and hashes are checked by the loader.

open_items.detail: The source states that livestock buildings should be located on the poorest soil. This is an oversimplified rule and could lead to unsuitable, poorly drained or inaccessible building sites.
open_items.required_action: Subject specialist must approve a site-selection explanation based on drainage, stability, access, water, hygiene, wind and biosecurity rather than a universal poorest-soil rule.

open_items.detail: The source places drip irrigation under overhead irrigation. Modern NRCS classification distinguishes sprinkler and micro-irrigation; drip is micro-irrigation, not an overhead sprinkler method.
open_items.required_action: Subject specialist must approve the corrected classification while preserving the source's intended sprinkler/drip comparison.

open_items.detail: The source lists removal of excess rainwater as an advantage of surface irrigation. Applying irrigation water and removing excess water by drainage are different operations.
open_items.required_action: Approve the corrected distinction and remove the drainage claim from the surface-irrigation advantages.

open_items.detail: The source suggests irrigation reduces salt accumulation without stating the necessary conditions. Irrigation water itself contains salts; leaching requires suitable water and adequate drainage.
open_items.required_action: Subject specialist must approve the qualified explanation of irrigation-water quality, leaching and drainage.

open_items.detail: The source lists the use of high-salt water as a disadvantage of drip irrigation, but the statement is ambiguous and technically incomplete. Saline water requires testing and specific management; it is not automatically suitable for drip systems.
open_items.required_action: Confirm the intended statement and approve guidance on water quality, emitter clogging, salt accumulation and leaching.

open_items.detail: Sixteen Week Six figures were found. Several are mobile screenshots of third-party pages and two drainage images include an Alamy stock photograph or screenshot; exact attribution and reuse permissions are not established.

open_items.detail: The source lists drought as a climate element. Drought is more accurately a climate-related hazard or period of water shortage; rainfall, temperature, humidity, wind and sunlight are climatic elements.
open_items.required_action: Subject specialist must approve the corrected distinction between climatic elements and drought.

open_items.detail: The source defines relative humidity simply as the amount of moisture in the atmosphere. This omits the saturation comparison and temperature dependence.
open_items.required_action: Approve the corrected definition as the ratio of actual to saturation water-vapour pressure at the same temperature, expressed as a percentage.

open_items.detail: The source places topography under edaphic factors. Topography is a physical or physiographic site factor rather than a soil property, although it affects agricultural production.
open_items.required_action: Subject specialist must approve the classification note and the expected answer for the topography multiple-choice item.

open_items.detail: The source states that sandy soil cannot support plant growth and clay soil prevents leaching. These are overly absolute; suitability depends on crop, management, soil structure, water and drainage.
open_items.required_action: Approve qualified explanations of sandy and clayey soil behaviour and remove universal claims of crop unsuitability.

open_items.detail: The source conflates sunshine duration, solar radiation and heat. These are related but distinct concepts.
open_items.required_action: Approve the distinction between solar energy, sunshine duration, photosynthesis and heat stress.

open_items.detail: The Week Seven assessment asks for effects of diseases, but the source body does not provide a dedicated disease subsection. An authored explanatory supplement has been added and requires subject review.
open_items.required_action: Verify and approve the disease definition, examples and effects before the lesson is released.

open_items.required_action: Provide the cited edition or replace the page reference with a verified accessible reading resource.

open_items.detail: The source nutrient table gives functions and deficiency symptoms only for nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium and magnesium, while the evaluation asks for sulphur, iron, manganese, copper, zinc, boron and molybdenum. Authored supplementary explanations have been added.
open_items.required_action: Subject specialist must verify and approve the added functions and deficiency symptoms for the seven requested nutrients before release.

open_items.detail: The source treats ammonification and nitrification as new nitrogen inputs and lists soil pH, oxidation and reduction as separate nitrogen-loss pathways. These are transformations or influencing conditions, not all external inputs or losses.
open_items.required_action: Approve the corrected separation of nitrogen inputs, transformations, plant uptake and loss pathways.

open_items.detail: The source gives a simplified carbon-cycle explanation and presents carbonates lost through leaching/drainage as a general pathway. The authored lesson qualifies this and adds carbon storage in soil, oceans and other reservoirs.
open_items.required_action: Subject specialist must approve the corrected carbon-cycle explanation and the role of soil carbon storage.

open_items.detail: The source lists plant and animal respiration as a main route for water entering the atmosphere but omits condensation and groundwater flow from its main explanation. Evaporation and transpiration are the principal land-to-atmosphere pathways.
open_items.required_action: Approve the completed water-cycle sequence and the distinction between transpiration, evaporation and respiration.
